title: Parodos (lines 156–213)

teacherSummary.text: The Chorus of Theban elders enters singing. They ask what Apollo's oracle will bring, describe the plague (crops failing, the dead lying unburied) and pray to Athenè, Artemis and Apollo to drive the destroying god away.

etymology.text: “infection”: Origin: Old French infection; earlier Late Latin īnfectiō.

context.history: The Chorus sang and danced in the orchestra. Its songs divide the play into episodes; this first entrance song is the parodos.

significance: The city speaks as one voice. The unburied dead show how far the plague has spread, and why the king must act.
discussionQuestions: How does a whole community react when it is afraid? Give a modern example.
Where does imagery appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with pride and fall?

items.prompt: Analyze the effect of the short, rhymed lines in “Wasted thus by death on death All our city perisheth”.

The phrase death on death piles loss upon loss, and the rhyme snaps shut on perisheth, so the couplet sounds final and relentless, like the plague itself. The form itself enacts the speed of the dying it describes.

satQuestions.passage:
Ah me, what countless woes are mine!
All our host is in decline;
Weaponless my spirit lies.
Earth her gracious fruits denies;
Women wail in barren throes;
Life on life downstricken goes,
Swifter than the wild bird’s flight,
Swifter than the Fire-God’s might,
To the westering shores of Night.
Wasted thus by death on death
All our city perisheth.
Corpses spread infection round;
None to tend or mourn is found.
Wailing on the altar stair
Wives and grandams rend the air—
Long-drawn moans and piercing cries
Blent with prayers and litanies.
Golden child of Zeus, O hear
Let thine angel face appear!

anchorPassages.note: The elders turn from human kingship to the gods as first defense.
anchorPassages.text:
Sweet-voiced daughter of Zeus from thy gold-paved Pythian shrine
Wafted to Thebes divine,
What dost thou bring me? My soul is racked and shivers with fear.
(Healer of Delos, hear!)
Hast thou some pain unknown before,
Or with the circling years renewest a penance of yore?
Offspring of golden Hope, thou voice immortal, O tell me.
First on Athenè I call; O Zeus-born goddess, defend!
Goddess and sister, befriend,
Artemis, Lady of Thebes, high-throned in the midst of our mart!
Lord of the death-winged dart!
Your threefold aid I crave
From death and ruin our city to save.
If in the days of old when we nigh had perished, ye drave
From our land the fiery plague, be near us now and defend us!

followUps: Which line from the scene does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: The Parodos turns the plague into the suffering of a whole people, which raises the stakes of the king's search. Useful evidence: “Wailing on the altar stair / Wives and grandams rend the air— / Long-drawn moans and piercing cries / Blent with prayers and litanies” (Parodos, lines 184–187): The sound of grief and prayer fills the scene, so the Chorus makes the reader hear the city's despair as well as see it. On structure: The Parodos is the Chorus's entrance song; it turns from the action of the Prologue to the feeling of the whole city, and it moves from a question about the oracle, through a picture of the plague, to a string of prayers. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

followUps: Which of your questions was hardest to answer from the text, and why?

items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: The Parodos turns the plague into the suffering of a whole people, which raises the stakes of the king's search. Useful evidence: “Sweet-voiced daughter of Zeus from thy gold-paved Pythian shrine / Wafted to Thebes divine” (Parodos, lines 156–157): The Chorus opens by asking what the oracle from Delphi will mean, mixing hope in the god with fear of his answer. Theme link: The Chorus speaks for the whole city at once, so the plague is shown as a shared suffering that the king and the gods are asked to end. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: The Parodos turns the plague into the suffering of a whole people, which raises the stakes of the king's search. Useful evidence: “Wasted thus by death on death / All our city perisheth. / Corpses spread infection round; / None to tend or mourn is found” (Parodos, lines 180–183): So many have died that the living cannot bury or mourn them, which shows how far the plague has broken the ordinary life of the city. Theme link: The Chorus speaks for the whole city at once, so the plague is shown as a shared suffering that the king and the gods are asked to end. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.
